genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a woman describes the path that led her to restoring paintings
her interest began while she was cleaning the workshop of a relative
at first she watched the yellowed layers being cleaned away
little by little she was allowed to work on parts of the painting
she set up her own premises in a courtyard once her training ended
her equipment includes a magnifying instrument and colours kept in jars
she has treated a family painting with a hole in it and a wall painting faded by water
she can spend several weeks on a very small surface
she says she finds it hard to consider a treatment finished
she teaches two beginners that the work must go unnoticed
text: It started with a broom. She was sweeping out an uncle's workshop, where damaged canvases came to be put right, and she stayed on to watch. The yellowed varnish lifted away under a damp swab of cotton, and to a child that looked like a conjuring trick. By her teens she was asking for a brush of her own. They handed her frames first, then a corner of sky, then a face. Once her training was over she rented a tiny place at the back of a courtyard, with a hinged magnifier and pigments kept in jars. Work came in slowly: a family portrait with a hole through it, a stairway mural that damp had turned grey. One painted palm, she admits, can keep her busy for weeks, and the hard part is knowing when to stop. She now has two apprentices, and tells them over and over that a good repair is one nobody notices.

units: the performance ends with a lukewarm response from the audience
the staging amounts to a dark rug and two seats
nothing painted appears on the stage
the lack of scenery leaves the audience without any clue about where the action happens
the script does not make up for this missing information
the musical accompaniment is played on the spot, hidden behind a hanging cloth
the sound covers the lines that are spoken quietly
one sequence carried by an actress is judged successful
the reviewer puts the failure down to excessive austerity
text: The audience filed out without much applause, and the chill in the room is easy enough to account for. Everything here rests on a bare stage: a dark rug, two stools, not a scrap of painted canvas. That could have thrown the whole weight onto the performers. It does the opposite, because the staging no longer tells us where we are. So we hunt the script for clues, the script gives up very few, and the story slips out of reach. Live music, played behind a hanging cloth, deepens the muddle: it swallows the quieter lines, and whole sentences go missing. One passage deserves rescuing, the second scene, where an actress plays a spell of mourning almost without moving; there, at last, the emptiness earns its keep. An evening undone by too much restraint rather than too little ambition.

units: the writer is writing from a workshop where wood is worked
a piano had been damaged by water
the keys were sticking and the sound was spoilt
a specialist had judged tuning impossible in that condition
the writer thought about getting rid of the instrument
a neighbour who works in wood offers to take it apart and dry it
the padding ruined by damp is replaced
the repair took up the two people through a cold season
the instrument now holds its tuning
the writer invites the reader to come and play it
text: I am writing from the joiner's workshop, among off-cuts, wood shavings and the smell of warm glue. You remember that old piano, the one the rain got into? I had given it up for lost. The keys stuck, the strings gave back a cracked sort of note, and the tuner I called said there was nothing to be done with it in that state. I nearly let it go for firewood. Then a neighbour who works in wood put another way to me: lift out the soundboard, dry the pieces flat under clamps, replace the felts that the damp had eaten. The two of us spent the whole winter on it, with no plan worth the name. Since the day before yesterday it holds its tuning. In the evenings I sit down and improvise clumsy things that nobody else will ever hear. Come and try it whenever you like; it is waiting for you.

units: the text sets sculpture made by taking material away against sculpture made by casting
carving does not let what has been removed be put back
the casting process starts from a model in clay
a hollow impression is taken from that model
metal or plaster is then poured into it
a cast piece can be made again for as long as the model survives
the carver must study the structure and the flaws of the block before starting
the caster must watch the tightness of the mould and the speed of setting
a carved surface keeps the mark of the tools
a cast piece shows lines where the parts of the mould met
text: What sets a carved sculpture apart from a cast one? Carving takes material away, and nothing puts it back; every stroke of the chisel is final. Casting runs the other way round: the maker shapes a model in clay, draws a hollow mould from it, then pours in metal or plaster, so the form can be had again for as long as the model lasts. Do the two ask for the same preparation? They do not. Carving means reading the block first, its grain and its hidden cracks, or the thing will split. Casting shifts the difficulty onto a tight mould and a rate of cooling held under control. And does the result look different? It does. Cut stone keeps the bite of the tool, while a cast piece carries thin ridges along the seams where the parts of the mould came together. The choice follows the effect you are after.

units: a museum official explains to visitors how a collection is built up
purchases follow a logic of completing a group already held
gifts raise the difficulty of the conditions set by the donor
some works are lent by another institution for a limited period
a visitor asks what becomes of the pieces that are never shown
objects not on display are kept in crates where the air is controlled
those pieces remain available for research work
a student asks what share of the collection can be seen
the official admits that the part on show is small
text: Standing by the central case, the keeper set out for his listeners, at some length, the way a collection comes together. He began with purchases: a museum rarely buys at random, and each fresh arrival has to round out a group already held. He turned next to gifts, which raise a delicate matter, since a donor commonly wants the bequest kept on permanent display. He mentioned loans as well, entrusted by another institution for a fixed term. A visitor then asked what became of the pieces that are never brought out at all. They sleep in store, he replied, in crates where the air is held steady, and scholars are free to work on them. A student wanted to know how much of the whole is on view. He granted that the share is small, and that no room, however grand, could reveal it all at once.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first tapestries answered practical needs of insulation and division
they also served to signal rank
the earliest patterns were geometric and repetitive
specialised workshops appear near the courts of the nobility
the hangings then begin to tell stories in pictures
the figures were recognised by the objects that went with them
dyeing improves and offers brighter colours
trade in these fabrics enriches merchant towns
a model painted by an artist was reproduced by unnamed workers
mechanisation reduced this craft to a narrow luxury trade
text: The earliest picture weaving grew out of plain need: to keep a cold wall at bay, to divide one room from the next, to mark rank. The patterns of that time were geometric, easy to repeat and easy to hold in the head. Then specialised workshops gathered around the courts of the nobility, and the hanging turned into a tale, whole scenes read from left to right, each figure known by the object it carried. Demand pushed the dyers to widen their range, and the glowing threads drawn from insects and from roots made the fortune of several trading towns. Later came the painted cartoon, laid down by an artist and then followed stitch by stitch by weavers who never signed their work. The arrival of the mechanical loom finally shrank this patient craft to a narrow trade in luxury goods.

units: the text explains why old paintings darken
the protective layer laid on the surface breaks down in contact with the air
that layer takes on a yellow tint which alters all the colours
how well the colouring matter lasts depends on where it comes from
colouring matter drawn from plants fades under too strong a light
the loss of one colour can change the tint of a whole area
deposits from burning form a greasy film over the work
what is seen today differs from the original appearance
these changes are what justify a careful cleaning
text: You have surely stood in front of an old painting at some point and wondered where that brownish haze comes from. Blame the varnish first of all. A coat goes on to shield the surface, but the film reacts with the air, turns yellow, and ends up tinting the whole picture like dirty glass. Then there are the pigments. Some colours hold for generations without shifting; others, drawn from plants, fade as soon as they get too much light, so a blue sky can drift towards green once the yellow that warmed it has gone. Add the soot from lamps and hearths, which settles as a fine greasy skin over the lot. The upshot is that the painting in front of you barely keeps the colour it had when it left the workshop. That is precisely why a clean carried out with caution is worth the trouble.

units: a water leak flooded the dressing room the night before the opening performance
the costumes were left soaked
the colours of a heavy cloth ran into pale garments
giving up the performance would have meant losing money
playing in rehearsal clothes was judged unacceptable
the technical manager suggests evening out the spoilt shades on purpose
every fabric is dipped again in one pale colour bath
the lighting is changed to suit these new shades
the audience knew nothing of the accident and enjoyed the result
the company has kept this version born of a mishap
text: The night before opening, a pipe gave way and the company found the dressing room under water, with the costumes lying in soaked heaps on the cold tiles. Dye from the heavy velvet cloaks had run into the pale shirts, and the stiffened collars hung limp. Calling it off would cost a great deal; going on in rehearsal clothes felt beneath them. The stage manager offered a way out that nobody expected: since the shades had bled anyway, why not let the whole stage look washed out. The team spent the night dipping every piece of cloth in one pale bath, until the range settled into an even greyish pink. The lighting crew cooled their lamps to suit. The audience, who knew nothing of the flood, praised a look that seemed coherent and bold. The company has played it that way ever since.

units: the text sets out two printmaking techniques to choose between
the first means cutting into a metal support
the metal is covered with a protective film before the drawing is made
a corrosive liquid deepens the lines opened with a point
the second technique calls for cutting away from a wood block the parts meant to stay white
this second method allows no correction
both processes involve inking the surface and then wiping it
the paper used must be dampened before it goes under the press
the hollow process gives a thick line that can be felt
the wood process gives even areas with sharp edges
text: Choose your road first, for two hands are held out to you and they ask for quite different kinds of patience. To work in hollow, take a metal plate under a thin coat of varnish, draw your lines through it with a point, then lower the plate into a biting bath: the acid eats down wherever you have opened the ground. To work in relief, take a block of soft wood and cut away everything that must come out white; here nothing at all can be taken back. Either way, ink the surface, wipe it clean, lay on damp paper and send the lot under the press. The eye tells the two apart soon enough. The hollow holds the ink and yields a dense line you can feel beneath a fingertip, while the wood gives flat areas and clean edges. Pull a first sheet, look hard at it, correct what jars, begin again.

units: a centre for preserving recordings has opened in a converted industrial building
a first station deals with magnetic tape
the tapes go through an oven before they are played
this heating stops the recording layer from clinging
a second station reads discs with an optical device that makes no contact
a third service writes the description of the sound documents
that description calls for listening to each recording right through
the security copies are spread over two sites
the manager judges the documentation more decisive than the medium itself
a recording without a description can no longer be found
text: A laboratory for sound preservation has just opened in a converted industrial hall, and the man in charge took us through the work station by station. The first station handles magnetic tape: the reels go into a drying oven before playback, so that the coating stops clinging to itself. The second deals with cut discs, whose grooves are read by an optical sensor that never touches them. The third looks after description, slow work, since every item has to be heard right through before it can be indexed. A fourth space, kept apart, holds the security copies, which are stored in two separate buildings. He comes back to one point: the medium matters less than the description file that travels with it, because an undescribed recording becomes unfindable and all but ceases to exist.
